projectNotes.text: The dry run surfaced two ordering gaps in the migration scripts. Both are fixed; the remaining risk is the rollback window, which needs a signed runbook before the cutover.

The benchmark review turned into a longer investigation than expected, so this note captures the full picture while it is fresh. The current query set was built from last quarter's support tickets, which means it over-represents short, navigational searches and under-represents the multi-step research queries that enterprise accounts actually run. We agreed to freeze a new set of forty queries: ten short navigational, ten long research, ten typo and stemming edge cases, and ten drawn from the Globex onboarding transcripts. The first pass of the new set shows a top-three hit rate of sixty-one percent, down from the eighty-four percent reported on the old set. That drop is not a regression in the search service; it is what happens when the benchmark stops flattering us. Two failure clusters stand out. The first is synonym collapse: queries that mix a product name with an internal acronym return documents from the wrong product family because the analyzer strips the acronym as a stop word. The second is recency bias: the ranking function boosts recently edited pages so aggressively that a two-year-old canonical runbook loses to a changelog entry that mentions the same terms once. We prototyped a synonym map for the twelve most common acronyms and a capped recency boost of one point five, and together they move the top-three rate to seventy-three percent with no measurable latency change. The remaining gap is mostly long research queries, where the bigger problem is chunking: we index whole pages, so a page that answers the query in one paragraph still competes against pages that mention every term in the title. The next experiment is passage-level indexing with a page-level rollup, but that is a larger change and needs an index-format migration. My recommendation is to ship the synonym map and the recency cap this sprint, keep the new benchmark set as the release gate, and schedule the passage-indexing spike for the following sprint. I also want a dashboard that tracks the top-three rate per query family so we notice when a single family regresses instead of watching one blended number move by a point and guessing why. None of this is committed yet; it is the shape of the proposal I will bring to the platform review on Thursday, and I would rather have the reasoning written down before the meeting than reconstruct it afterward.

The trial cohort reached first value faster than the last one, mostly because the empty state now points at a sample project. Next question is whether the pricing page should appear before or after the first saved entry.
